title: Na⁺ Ion Migration through Glass, Encapsulant, and ARC

key_findings.detail:
Three principal Na⁺ sources have been identified:

1. **Front cover glass (soda-lime glass):** Contains ~12–15 wt% Na₂O; the dominant long-term source
2. **Cell surface contamination:** Baseline Na⁺ surface contamination of **$7.0 \times 10^{13}$ atoms/cm$^2$** is present on commercial cells prior to encapsulation; this is the fastest-acting source (PID visible within 1 day)
3. **EVA encapsulant:** Na can leach from glass through EVA and accumulate at cell; transit time through 900 µm EVA is **3–7 days**

- [[papers/AIP-127-2944-2-s2.0-85056609634-2018-J-Origin of Na causing potential-induced degradation for p-type crystalline Si photovoltaic modules.pdf#page=1|Jonai & Masuda (2018), p.1]]

Under applied field, Na⁺ drift through 80 nm PECVD SiNx follows Stern-Eyring hopping kinetics:

- **Without field:** thermal diffusion time for Na⁺ across 80 nm SiNx ≈ **1 million years**
- **With 0.5 MV/cm field at 80°C:** transit time ≈ **25 minutes**
- **Drift velocity:** $v = \mu E$ (mobility × electric field), with activation energy **0.51 eV** in SiNx
- [[papers/Elsevier-564-3774-2-s2.0-84940452054-2015-J-Drift characteristics of mobile ions in SiNx films and solar cells.pdf#page=2|Wilson et al. (2015), p.2]]

Na⁺ drift through the module stack follows three temporal phases (Schulze et al., 2020):

- **Phase 1 (constant current):** Low, time-independent current from surface contamination and small holes in SiNx
- **Phase 2 (accelerated):** Electric field builds across SiNx as Na⁺ accumulates at outer surface; current increases exponentially following: $J_{Na} \propto \sinh(\gamma E)$. At 49°C/1000 V this phase spans ~40 hours; at 90°C/1000 V it spans **1.73 hours**
- **Phase 3 (recovery):** After voltage removal, Na⁺ decays via one-dimensional diffusion $\propto 1/t^{0.5}$

- [[papers/IEEE-164-2299-2-s2.0-85087499813-2020-J-A Drift and Diffusion Model for PID-s in Solar Modules.pdf#page=2|Schulze et al. (2020), p.2]]

key_findings.claim: Na⁺ Accumulation at the Si/SiNx Interface
key_findings.detail:
Na⁺ accumulates at the Si/SiNx interface and in the silicon cell:

- Peak Na concentration after PID stress: **$\sim 10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$** (a few atomic %) measured by dynamic SIMS
- Na area density within stacking fault planes: **$\sim 10^{15}$ cm$^{-2}$**
- Na onset drift temperature: **~50°C**, overlapping with normal module operating temperatures
- Na drift peak temperature in SiNx: **~115°C**
- [[papers/AIP-127-2944-2-s2.0-85056609634-2018-J-Origin of Na causing potential-induced degradation for p-type crystalline Si photovoltaic modules.pdf#page=4|Jonai & Masuda (2018), p.4]]
- [[papers/Elsevier-564-3774-2-s2.0-84940452054-2015-J-Drift characteristics of mobile ions in SiNx films and solar cells.pdf#page=3|Wilson et al. (2015), p.3]]

Na⁺ diffusion occurs in both EVA and ionomer encapsulants, but only EVA leads to PID, confirming that Na⁺ arrival is necessary but not sufficient — the encapsulant's ability to transmit ions to the cell surface determines PID outcome:

- Na concentration after PID in EVA: **$\sim 10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$** (few atomic %)
- EVA resistivity: ~$10^{14}$ Ω·cm; Ionomer: ~$10^{16}$ Ω·cm; Polyolefin: ~$10^{17}$ Ω·cm
- Modules with ionomer encapsulant maintained stable Pmax despite confirmed Na diffusion through ionomer
- [[papers/IOP-53-3675-2-s2.0-84956692262-2016-J-Consideration on Na diffusion and recovery phenomena in potential-induced degradation for crystallin.pdf#page=2|Masuda et al. (2016), p.2]]

In PERC cells, the SiO₂ passivation layer between the emitter and SiNx controls whether Na⁺ can disrupt the ARC:

- **Thin SiO₂ (1 nm) with high-RI SiNx (n=2.2):** enables electron tunneling that dissipates charge, nearly eliminating PID (~1% degradation)
- **Thick SiO₂ (9 nm):** blocks electron tunneling regardless of SiNx RI; both RI=2.0 and 2.2 show identical rapid PID (10–15% power loss)
- **Critical threshold:** ~2 nm SiO₂ where RI effects begin to emerge
- [[papers/Wiley-178-1653-2-s2.0-85127380886-2022-J-Effects of SiNx refractive index and SiO2 thickness on polarization-type potential-induced degradati.pdf#page=1|Wang et al. (2022), p.1]]
